column1: # The complete Flotilla demo: <caption><TAB><what Kit says>. Captions must match full-demo.sh's caption: steps (unique, no semicolons).

column2: Coding agents, each alone in its own isolated cloud VM. All in one window on your Mac. This is Flotilla.

column1: Hold to merge, at a glance
column2: And when the work is done, you hold to merge.

Every thread is a conversation with a coding agent, running in its own boat dot dev VM. The sidebar sorts them by what needs you. Unread replies come first, then idle threads. Working and archived wait at the bottom.
A row is the title, the agent's last reply in a line or two, and the agent and model underneath. Nothing about the VM, unless it needs you.
Drag the edge to make the sidebar wider, or hide it to a slim rail, and bring it back the same way.
With nothing open, the main area is a new thread, ready for a prompt.
Pick any agent and model that boat offers. Claude Code, Codex, Open Code, Kimi, and more, each with its own effort levels.
With no project, the thread gets a blank VM. I'll ask Haiku, a small and quick model, for a little script.
The thread opens straight away. The VM takes a few seconds to start, then the agent's words and tool calls stream in as it works.
A small model on this Mac writes the title from the first prompt.
Up top, the VM's time left before it stops itself. The model sits by the message box.
While a turn runs, the message box steers it. What you send joins the turn already under way, without starting over.
The agent picks the steer up and changes course.
Stop interrupts a turn. Nothing is lost, and you can send again whenever you like.
Threads run side by side, with any mix of agents. This one is Codex, on a small model.
Working threads gather at the bottom, each with its timer.
When one finishes, a toast says so, and its row gets an unread mark and a one line summary of the reply, written by the same small model.
Hover a row for the rest: the agent and model, the VM, and when it will stop.
Command one to nine jump straight to a thread.
Hover a reply to copy it. Right click to cite it, and the quote lands in the message box, ready for your answer.
Code blocks have their own copy button.
Long prompts fold away, and the up arrow brings back the last one you sent.
Idle VMs stop on their own after five, ten or thirty minutes, so a thread costs nothing while you're away.
A stopped VM keeps its disk. Send to it, and it wakes up and carries on where it left off.
The cup keeps a VM running, for when something long is going on in it.
And preview opens any port in the VM, in your browser.
Double click a title to rename it, or let the model suggest one.
Archive stops the VM and keeps the history. Changed your mind? Undo.
Sending to an archived thread brings it back.
Delete removes the VM and the thread for good, after asking first.
Projects are GitHub repos. Flotilla talks to GitHub through the G H command line tool you're already signed in with.
Add project lists your repos. This one is a small retry library, with a web page that draws its backoff.
The repo has a dot agents setup script, so Flotilla runs it to prepare the project's VM. Scripts you add here run just before it.
The first setup clones the repo and runs the script. Every new thread will start from a copy of this VM.
Ready. Flotilla checks main every minute, and prepares each new commit in the background.
Each project thread gets a VM of its own, with the repo set up from the latest main. It can also start on any branch or open pull request.
A small model names the branch from the prompt.
The thread copies the prepared VM, switches to its branch, and reruns setup, which takes seconds when nothing changed.
The repo's services file starts its web app in the background, and Preview lists it, ready to open.
Here's what the agent is working on: a retry visualizer.
The agent opened a draft pull request. Its bar sits on the message box, with the checks, the changes, and what to do next.
Meanwhile, a teammate changed the same line on main. The header says the branch is one behind, and the conflict shows in red.
Resolve writes a prompt for the agent and puts it in the message box. Nothing is sent until I press send.
The agent rebased and pushed, and the checks are green.
Ready for review, then hold to merge. The button fills as you hold. Let go early and nothing happens.
Merged. Flotilla sees it, and prepares the new main straight away.
When a check fails, Fix writes a prompt with what failed.
And when a commit breaks setup on main, the setup run fails, and new threads keep starting from the last good one.
Fix in a new thread opens a thread with the commit, the failing script, its exit code, and the end of its log.
The thread starts even though setup fails, so the agent can fix it.

column1: # 12. Start from a branch or PR

column2: Any branch or open pull request can be a starting point. Search, type a number, or paste a link.
And any project thread can hand its branch to a new thread, from its menu.
Four files in dot agents tell Flotilla how to set up, wake, clean up, and serve the repo. It's the same convention as Amp's orbs.
Resume runs when a stopped VM wakes, for quick work like signing back in. It gets ten seconds.
Archive runs when a thread is archived, to remove what it made outside the VM, like a database branch.
And services run the dev servers, with their output and a restart a click away.
Settings holds the defaults: the agent for new threads, the idle stop, a branch prefix, and the model that writes titles. Your key stays in the keychain, and the history in a database on your Mac.
That's Flotilla. A fleet of coding agents, each in its own boat, all in one window.
With a few projects going, the filter narrows the list. Just one project, just the threads with no project, or everything.
Services make a change easy to see. Here's the visualizer as it is on main.
I'll ask Haiku to retitle the two timelines, so the point lands at a glance.
The agent edits the page, rebuilds it, runs the tests, and opens a draft pull request.
And here's the page with its new titles, on the agent's branch.
Put it together, and one project can have a fleet going at once. Each agent alone in its own VM. Claude and Codex, side by side.
Hover any of them for its agent and its VM. Each one's pull request lands in its bar when it's ready.
Click the checks to see each one, with a link to its run on GitHub.
A thread's menu opens its pull request on GitHub, copies its branch name, or links a different pull request.
The project page keeps every setup run: what started it, how long it took, and what failed.
The scripts you add here run before the repo's own setup. Run setup again, or rebuild from scratch, any time.
And View log shows a setup run's whole output, script by script, for when something needs a closer look.
Flotilla follows your Mac between light and dark, in the plum, coral, amber and lavender of its icon.
